intro/hello: Welcome to reinforcement learning for language models.
intro/imitate: Everything so far has taught a model to imitate. Pretraining copies the web, and fine-tuning copies answers that people wrote.
intro/target: Imitation needs a target: someone has to write the right answer first.
intro/judge: But many things are easier to judge than to write. A program can check a math answer; a person can pick the better reply.
intro/rl: Reinforcement learning learns from that judgment. The model tries an answer, gets a score, and shifts its probabilities toward what scored well.
intro/number: The score is just a number. No target, no gradient, no explanation.
intro/next: This lecture builds the toolkit on a toy small enough to see completely, and the next three chapters stand on it: P P O, D P O and G R P O.
intro/go: So let us look at a language model the way reinforcement learning sees it.
policy/words: Reinforcement learning has its own vocabulary, but each word has a plain meaning for a language model.
policy/state: The state is the prompt, plus every token written so far. Our prompt asks: is ninety one prime?
policy/policy: The policy is the model itself. Given the state, its softmax gives a probability to every possible next token.
policy/policyname: Policy is the reinforcement learning word for a rule that picks actions: here, the next token.
policy/action: And an action is the token it picks.
policy/tree: Picture every possible answer as a tree. Each branch is one choice, labeled with the policy's probability.
policy/walk: Sampling walks down the tree: No, with probability one half, then seven times thirteen, with probability zero point four.
policy/episode: One full walk is one episode: a complete answer.
policy/reward: Only at the very end does the answer get its reward: one score for the whole thing.
policy/grades: Our grader gives one point for a right answer with a reason, half a point for a bare right answer, and nothing for a wrong one.
policy/trap: Ninety one looks prime, but it is seven times thirteen, so this model answers wrongly half of the time.
logprob/chain: The probability of a whole answer is a product: the first token's probability, times the second's, given the first.
logprob/prod: For our path, one half times zero point four gives zero point two.
logprob/long: Real answers are hundreds of tokens long, and a product of that many numbers below one races toward zero.
logprob/under: Eleven hundred tokens at one half each, and the computer rounds the answer to exactly zero. It underflows.
logprob/logs: Logarithms fix this, because the log of a product is the sum of the logs.
logprob/scale: The log of one is zero. The log of one half is about minus zero point six nine. The log of a tiny probability is a large negative number.
logprob/sum: So instead of multiplying tiny numbers, we add moderate negative ones. Eleven hundred tokens give about minus seven hundred and sixty. No problem.
logprob/star: That sum is the log probability of the answer, and it is the star of this lecture.
expected/bandit: Now collapse the tree, and treat each complete answer as one action: four answers, each with a probability and a grade.
expected/name: One choice and one reward is called a bandit, after slot machines. Ours has four arms.
expected/random: Sampling is random, so the reward changes every time. Which number should training push up?
expected/average: The average: sample thousands of answers, grade them all, and take the mean. That is the expected reward.
expected/weighted: An expected value is just a weighted average: every answer's reward, weighted by how often the policy writes it.
expected/calc: Here that is zero point three times one half, plus zero point two times one, which makes zero point three five.
expected/huge: A real model can write more answers than there are atoms in the universe, so we can never add them all up.
expected/sample: But we can sample. Draw answers from the policy, grade them, and average the grades.
expected/settle: With a few samples, the average jumps around. With hundreds, it settles onto zero point three five.
expected/recipe: Sample, score, average. Everything that follows is built to be estimated this way.
trick/goal: To improve the policy, we want the gradient of the expected reward: the direction in weight space that raises the average grade.
trick/diff: Write it as a sum over answers of probability times reward, and differentiate. The rewards do not depend on the weights; only the probabilities do.
trick/snag: And now we are stuck. Without the probability weights, the sum is no longer an average over samples, and we cannot add up every answer.
trick/trick: Here is the trick. The gradient of a probability equals the probability, times the gradient of its log.
trick/chain: It is only the chain rule. The derivative of log u is one over u, times the derivative of u. Multiply both sides by u, and there it is.
trick/back: Substitute it in, and the probability weight is back in front.
trick/pg: So the gradient of the expected reward is itself an average: of the reward, times the gradient of the log probability.
trick/recipe: And that we can estimate: sample answers, find the direction that makes each one more likely, scale it by its reward, and average.
trick/black: And the reward never needs a gradient. It can come from a program, a reward model, or a person.
trick/heart: This one line is the policy gradient, and it sits under all of post-training.
softmax/left: One ingredient is left: the gradient of the log probability. For a softmax policy, it is simple.
softmax/logits: Give each answer a logit, a raw score, and turn the logits into probabilities with a softmax, like the class scores of a linear classifier.
softmax/formula: The gradient of log pi of y, with respect to the logits, is the one-hot vector for y, minus the probabilities.
softmax/read: Read it as an instruction: raise the sampled answer's logit, and lower every other logit by its own probability.
softmax/example: If we sampled No, seven times thirteen, its logit goes up by zero point eight, and the others go down by their probabilities.
softmax/zero: The pushes add up to zero. Probability only moves around; it is never created.
softmax/ce: You have seen this before, with the sign flipped: a softmax classifier's cross-entropy gradient was probabilities minus the one-hot label.
softmax/supervised: So a policy gradient step is a supervised step on the model's own sample, as if it were the correct label.
softmax/scaled: With one difference: the step is scaled by the reward. A great answer is learned strongly, and a poor one barely at all.
softmax/tokens: A language model ends in a softmax over its vocabulary, so the same formula holds at every token.
reinforce/name: Put the pieces together, and you have the oldest policy gradient algorithm: reinforce, from Ronald Williams in nineteen ninety two.
reinforce/loop: Sample an answer, grade it, and step uphill along reward times the gradient of its log probability. Repeat.
reinforce/start: Watch it on our bandit. The policy starts as the base model, with forty percent on the wrong yes.
reinforce/steps: Each step samples one answer, ringed in gold, and nudges the logits.
reinforce/wrong: Sampling a wrong answer changes nothing at all, because its reward is zero.
reinforce/right: Sampling a rewarded answer pushes it up, and everything else down.
reinforce/drift: Step by step, the policy drifts toward the best answer, and the expected reward climbs.
reinforce/noisy: But look at the path: it is jagged, and every run would take a different one.
reinforce/loss: In practice, we write a surrogate loss, minus the reward times the log probability, and let autograd do the rest.
reinforce/weighted: It is cross-entropy on the model's own samples, weighted by reward, and the reward is a plain constant, with no gradient through it.
baselines/noise: reinforce works, but it is noisy, and the noise has a specific cause.
baselines/all: The update pushes up every sampled answer, in proportion to its reward, but the useful signal lives in the differences between rewards.
baselines/runs: Here are eight runs with different seeds. They already disagree a little.
baselines/shift: Now add two points to every reward. Every answer gets pushed up, the good ones only slightly more than the bad.
baselines/fan: On average, the gradient is exactly the same. But the eight runs fan out.
baselines/stuck: Some lock onto a worse answer for good: whatever they sampled got pushed up, became likelier, and got sampled again.
baselines/fix: The fix is to judge each reward against what you expected. Subtract a baseline, b.
baselines/adv: Reward minus baseline is the advantage, A: how much better than usual was this answer?
baselines/why: Why is this allowed? Probabilities always add up to one, so the gradient of the log probability averages to zero: pushes up and down cancel.
baselines/free: So subtracting b times it changes nothing on average. It only removes noise.
baselines/tight: With a running mean as the baseline, the eight runs pull back together, shift or no shift.
baselines/teach: And an answer worse than usual is now pushed down, so even a wrong answer teaches something.
baselines/family: The best baseline is close to the average reward. A running mean, the group mean in G R P O, and the value function in P P O all estimate it.
credit/tokens: A real answer is hundreds of tokens, and the reward arrives once, at the end.
credit/which: So which tokens deserve the credit?
credit/sum: The log probability of an answer is a sum over its tokens, so the policy gradient has one term per token.
credit/same: And with one reward at the end, every token of an answer gets the same advantage.
credit/rows: Here are sampled answers: an opener, some work, and a verdict. Only the verdict is graded.
credit/tint: Each chunk is tinted by its answer's advantage: green above average, red below.
credit/filler: The filler, let me think, is pushed up in good answers and down in bad ones.
credit/average: Average each chunk's push over more and more answers, and the filler nets out to zero. It never mattered.
credit/work: Working out seven times thirteen earns real credit, because it usually leads to the right verdict. Saying ninety one is odd earns blame.
credit/stats: Credit assignment emerges statistically. The price is noise, and more of it the longer the answers get.
credit/value: A sharper tool is a value function: it predicts the final grade from a partial answer, and credits each token with the change it caused.
credit/jump: Here the predicted grade jumps from zero point five four to zero point nine at seven times thirteen. That is P P O's critic, next chapter.
kl/hack: Optimize a reward hard enough, and the policy finds whatever the reward likes most, which is not always what we meant.
kl/rm: Say a learned reward model has a blind spot: it scores a shouted answer at one point two, above the genuinely best one.
kl/rare: The reference model almost never writes it, three percent of the time, and its true quality is zero.
kl/leash: The fix is a leash. Keep a frozen copy of the starting model, the reference policy, and charge the policy for moving away from it.
kl/kl: The distance is the K L divergence: averaged over the policy's own answers, the log of how much likelier the policy finds them than the reference.
kl/penalty: It is charged inside the reward: the reward, minus beta times that log ratio. reinforce needs no change.
kl/opt: For a bandit, the best policy has a closed form: the reference, reweighted by e to the reward over beta.
kl/loose: Let the leash go slack, with a tiny beta, and the policy abandons everything for the hack: the reward model's score climbs, and true quality collapses.
kl/tight: Pull it tight, with a large beta, and the policy barely leaves the reference.
kl/sweet: In between, around zero point two, the policy gets the most true quality.
kl/dpo: Remember that formula. Chapter sixteen turns it around to derive D P O.
entropy/only: One more failure, a quieter one. reinforce can only reinforce answers the policy actually samples.
entropy/start: Start from a base model that rarely explains itself: the best answer gets only five percent.
entropy/squeeze: A decent, common answer gets sampled, pushed up, and squeezes the rare one further.
entropy/runs: Twelve runs. About half find the best answer. The other half lock onto a plain no, for good.
entropy/never: Once the best answer's probability is near zero, it is never sampled again, so it can never earn credit.
entropy/entropy: The measure of this is entropy: the average surprise of the policy's own samples.
entropy/range: It is zero when the policy always writes the same thing, and largest when it spreads evenly.
entropy/crash: In the stuck runs, the entropy crashes within a few dozen steps.
entropy/bonus: A small entropy bonus pays the policy to stay a little uncertain, so it keeps trying the alternatives.
entropy/found: With a bonus of zero point one, all twelve runs find the best answer.
entropy/much: Too much, and the policy stays random. In language model training, entropy is watched closely: a fast collapse is a warning sign.
outro/recap: Here is the whole recipe on one screen.
outro/grade: Grade them, with any score you like.
outro/kl: Subtract a K L penalty, to stay close to the reference.
outro/adv: Subtract a baseline, to turn rewards into advantages.
outro/loss: And step along the advantage, times the gradient of the log probability.
outro/rlhf: The next chapters swap in better parts. R L H F learns the reward from human preferences, and P P O adds a critic and clipped steps that reuse samples.
outro/dpo: D P O skips the sampling loop entirely, using the closed form of the leash.
outro/grpo: And G R P O grades with a program, and uses a group of answers to the same prompt as its baseline.
outro/explore: All three keep this same core: sample, grade, and raise the log probability of whatever beat the baseline. First up, R L H F.
